comments.author: @BTinSF
comments.text: Ask yourself why the homeless live on the sidewalks of one limited San Francisco neighborhood.  Among the reasons: (1) San Francisco is incredibly tolerant of "alternative" lifestyles and always has been--it does not punish things other cities do including things many Americans would argue it should (once that was homosexuality, now it's drug use and "living rough"; (2) the city is amazingly wealthy and thus offers services and even cash to indigents (it spends something like $80,000 per year on each one of them), (3) the weather never gets oppressively hot nor frigid and snow is almost unknown so outdoor living can be made comfortable all year round.  Unfortunately for the city and its working, tax-paying residents, large parts of America sends their rejects to the west coast and especially San Francisco where they find a niche.

replies.author: @BTinSF
replies.text:
The ugly Villaincourt fountain at that plaza on the Embarcadero is finally being removed and the entire area is in a process of redevelopment.  Plans for that are still under discussion.   Bloomingdales, Macy's, and the other department stores are disappearing because nobody shops at department stores in the age of online shopping.  It is a dead business model and not just in San Francisco.  The buildings will be repurposed.  There is an active program to bring educational institutions downtown.  Vanderbilt U (of Tennessee) has already agreed to establish a new campus in the city.  There will be others.  San Francisco is now the AI/tech capital of the world and schools want to have a presence there as do financial institutions and so on.
I've lived in the city for 44 years and the entire time people have been saying "it's not like it used to be".

comments.author: @woodedlane
comments.text: The cable cars were put in because the rich wanted the best view on top of Nob Hill and horse and carriage could not get up there.  If you ever visit Sf, the cable car museum is a must see.  The sea lions moved in after the 89 Loma prieta quake.  Initially they tried to get them to leave but finally gave in and they've been at Pier 39 ever since.  It's like they wanted to be the next tourist attraction.  And if you visit and take the cable car, the best one is the Powell/Hyde because it takes you up above crooked Lombard where there are great views.  The Powell/Mason ends up at the same place, but from a lower route.  SF has this thing about roof space for high rises for the public.  Check out public roof tops - and Salesforce Tower has a whole upscale garden path that goes for blocks.  Just so much to see and experience here.  I love my city of the last 40 years.  Just a nice bunch of people from every corner of the Earth hanging out together laughing eating and sharing stories.  I started out on a farm in the midwest and am very happy I ended up here.  And finally, not 10 blocks from where I live is a French bakery that Bon appetit named as best in the U.S. and I would have to agree. :)
